meta.title: DoorDash: Buying the Volume for a Warehouse
meta.dek: Orders grew 28% and GAAP profit nearly doubled in the quarter the company agreed to pay $17 billion for Instacart. Management says the deal exists to give its own warehouses enough volume to pay. What does $178 assume, and does the volume earn its price?

verdict.sentence: DoorDash grew orders 28% and agreed to buy Instacart for about $17 billion to give its DashMart warehouses the volume they need, but at $178.26 the probability-weighted case pays [[pw_return]] a year against the 13% hurdle: Watch.
verdict.breaks_if: The grocery bet fails to pay: New Verticals is still not gross-profit positive in the Q4 2026 letter, or the Instacart deal closes with DoorDash's investment-grade rating lost or the stock consideration above the 25% cap. Then the largest deal in the company's history buys volume without profit.
verdict.next: Q4 ~mid-Feb 2027 · Instacart vote and antitrust clearance (dates TBD)
verdict.price_implies: between the Base and the Bull (GAAP EPS ≈[[Priced-in.eps]] in 2031 for 9%/yr)

call: The business is stronger than in August. Q3 orders grew 28% (17% without Deliveroo), contribution profit reached 5.2% of GOV and adjusted EBITDA was $1.06 billion, above the midpoint of the guide for the third quarter running. The stock is 24% lower, at $178.26. At that price a 9% return needs GAAP EPS of [[Priced-in.eps]] in 2031 at 24 times, a third of the way from my Base ([[Base.eps]]) to my Bull, and 13% needs [[Hurdle.eps]]. The probability-weighted value is [[pw_ev]], a return of [[pw_return]] a year, and the price that returns 13% is [[entry]]. The price implies a Bear probability of only [[implied_bear]]. What the market may have wrong is the Instacart deal: it is about $17 billion, at least $12.75 billion of it in cash, bought to give a warehouse business, DashMart, volume it cannot disclose the cost of, and DoorDash says it will reinvest more than 100% of the synergies in year one. I value the deal at no value created. The number that proves or breaks it is New Verticals gross profit, which the CFO says is 'pretty close to breakeven' and is committed to turn positive by the end of 2026.

tests.claim: That New Verticals, DashMart included, pays for itself.
tests.test: A statement in the Q4 2026 letter or call (about mid-February 2027) that New Verticals was gross-profit positive for Q4 or the second half. At the Q3 call the CFO said 'We are pretty close to being breakeven on a gross profit level' and had committed to positive by year end.
tests.if_fail: 10 points Base → Bear (PW EV [[test1.pw_ev]], [[test1.pw_return]]/yr) → **Watch / Hold**, entry ≤[[test1.entry]].

tests.claim: That the core keeps turning growth into profit.
tests.test: Q4 2026 adjusted EBITDA of at least $1.0 billion (guide $0.9–1.1 billion; Q3 was $1,060 million) and Q4 Marketplace GOV of at least $35.4 billion, both in the Q4 release (about mid-February 2027), with FY2026 GAAP operating margin of at least 6% in the 10-K.
tests.if_fail: 10 points Base → Bear (PW EV [[test2.pw_ev]], [[test2.pw_return]]/yr) → **Watch / Hold**, entry ≤[[test2.entry]].

tests.claim: That the deal is financed and cleared on the announced terms.
tests.test: Through the Q2 2027 10-Q (early August 2027): DoorDash keeps an investment-grade rating (it has said it is targeting one), stock consideration stays within the 25% cap, and no antitrust remedy or repricing changes what DoorDash is buying. The deal is not expected to close until the end of 2027 or the first half of 2028, so this is a test of the path, not the close.
tests.if_fail: 15 points Base → Bear (PW EV [[test3.pw_ev]], [[test3.pw_return]]/yr) → **Watch / Hold**, entry ≤[[test3.entry]].

return_math.compounding: Base GAAP EPS compounds from ≈$2.83 in FY2026 to [[Base.eps]] in FY2031, [[Base.cagr]] a year, with no dividend: that is the compounding rate at a flat multiple, and it is high because FY2026 is a thin-margin base (operating margin ≈7%) that the Base takes to ≈15%. Re-rating takes about 22 points a year off the Base return, because the exit at 24× is far below today's ≈63× FY2026 GAAP EPS. All of the gap to the hurdle is the multiple.
return_math.price_implied: At 9%, spot needs GAAP EPS of [[Priced-in.eps]] in FY2031 at 24×: revenue near $38B and an operating margin near 17%, between my Base and Bull. At 13% it needs [[Hurdle.eps]].
return_math.epv: Earnings power today is thin on GAAP numbers: TTM operating income of $0.90B taxed at 21% is ≈$0.71B, or ≈$8B capitalized at 9%, plus ≈$4.1B of net cash: ≈$12B, about $28 a share. On adjusted EBITDA less stock compensation and about $0.75B of capex, taxed at 21%, it is ≈$18B, about $42 a share. Neither is a floor for a business that is reinvesting for growth; both show how much of the $178 is growth.
return_math.base_rate: Revenue of ≈$18B sits in the $12–25B bucket. The Base's 15% nominal growth (≈12.5% real) was achieved over five years by about 15% of companies this size; the Bull's 19% (≈16.5% real) by about 7%. Credit Suisse HOLT, 1950–2015, ([Base Rate Book](https://sorfis.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/The-Base-Rate-Book-Integrating-the-Past-to-Better-Anticipate-the-Future-September-2016.pdf)); survivorship makes the true odds somewhat lower.
return_math.terminal_growth: Implied perpetual growth on GAAP earnings at 9%: Bull [[Bull.g]], Base [[Base.g]], Bear [[Bear.g]], against a 4.88% ten-year Treasury yield (FRED, Nov 9, 2026). The Bull sits above it, so it is a stretch case.
return_math.year_ten: Still growing at about 10% a year at the end of the Base, and the exit multiple assumes that continues into year ten; if growth falls to mid-single digits the multiple is doing the work.
return_math.rr_note: The downside is share loss plus an unearned Instacart price at a normal multiple, not a broken business.
return_math.note: Computed rows come from model.json. Segment margin rows are gross margins after cost of revenue (excluding D&A), applied equally to both geographies `[Estimate]`; 'Corporate and other' is all other operating expense, D&A and restructuring. The Instacart acquisition is not in any case.
